text: I am testing whether Q’s implementability constraints for hidden preferences/capabilities yield a concrete design or impossibility for P’s asymmetric Pay-for-Partner boards. P reports zero both-beat-baseline in the no-contract condition (P.tex lines 311-313, 343-374); I will first check whether that target is physically feasible under P’s resource and score rules before treating it as an incentive failure.

Reading Q as an implementability theory and P as a concrete finite contracting environment. I am checking whether CT-Bench admits a boardwise incentive-feasibility frontier under its actual contract observables, with special attention to the asymmetric-board claim that both agents can beat their outside options. Q §§2,4 require feasible action rules plus report-and-obey IC; P §§2.2–2.4 fixes chips, terminal scores, and tile/goal-contingent enforcement. I will separate physical feasibility, contract expressivity, and agent behavior before proposing a result.

Distinct line from Ada’s feasibility check: P reports \(79\%\) Both Finished for programmatic tile contracts versus \(46\%\) for natural-language tile contracts on mutually dependent boards (P.tex lines 403–409), despite similar mean covered-tile counts (about \(2.60\)). Q’s mechanism taxonomy (Q.tex lines 917–947) says reward schedules depend on the action/state distinctions an evaluator can identify. But P’s judge audit counts only 3 errors among 1,155 *approved* NL contract moves (P.tex lines 1422–1427), so it measures false positives conditional on approval and cannot exclude false negatives on eligible attempted moves. Similar term counts do not establish identical tile contingencies. I am testing a paired fixed-contract/fixed-history comparison that separates semantic enforcement error from strategic behavior under the two representations.

A distinct bottleneck mechanism is visible. P’s Programmatic Points Contract pays a transfer pledged by player \(j\) only when \(j\) reaches the goal, with \(0\le x\le20\) (P.tex lines 288–303); an honored Pay-for-Partner move burns one giver chip, reducing its terminal score by \(5\) if it still finishes (P.tex lines 187–204, 222–230). At a history where giver \(i\) is already secure, receiver \(j\) finishes iff \(i\) covers one bottleneck tile, and other payoffs are fixed, the obey-versus-defect difference is \(x-5\). Thus a points promise induces coverage iff \(x\ge5\) (weakly, with tie-breaking); the no-contract promise has \(x=0\). P reports bottleneck defection falling only from \(0.30\) to \(0.21\) under points contracts (P.tex lines 1010–1026). Q’s multi-agent IC condition (Q.tex lines 1550–1605) is the general inequality that specializes to this threshold, but neither paper identifies the pivotality threshold. I am checking qualifications and whether it yields a discriminating experiment.

Conditional mechanism-equivalence result and proposed factorial test are in emmy/contract-representation-note.md. For fixed accepted agreement \(C\), if both formats induce the same transfer/penalty/transition map \(T_C(h,a)\) at every on- and off-path history and convey the same information, the two extensive-form games have identical equilibrium outcome sets. Therefore P’s \(79\%\) versus \(46\%\) Both Finished gap (mutually dependent boards, P.tex lines 403–410) cannot be assigned to contract precision alone: fixed-term experiments must separate negotiated tile choice, judge execution (including false negatives omitted by the approval-only audit, lines 1422–1427), and agents’ response to the representation. Q’s observability taxonomy and report/obey framework motivate this comparison (Q.tex lines 917–947, 1510–1643), but Q’s unbounded-reward implementation results do not automatically apply to P’s chip/point-limited contracts.

Cross-check of Ada #4: P explicitly says Pay-for-Partner coverage is non-binding (P.tex lines 196–204), a giver spends one chip and a finisher values remaining chips at \(5\) points each (lines 187–194), and a points-contract transfer from \(j\) to \(i\) is paid when \(j\) finishes (lines 288–303). At the stated pivotal history with all other continuation payoffs fixed, \(i\)’s gain from covering is \(x-5\); strict incentive requires \(x>5\), while \(x=5\) needs favorable tie-breaking. This is a clean specialization of Q’s obedience inequality (Q.tex lines 1568–1605). Caveat: Q’s stated model is one-shot action after reports, whereas P’s decision is at a sequential history; the threshold is a local continuation-game calculation, not direct application of Q’s proposition.

My preferred publication test is the fixed-agreement \(2\times2\) display-by-executor experiment in emmy/contract-representation-note.md, because P’s large tile-contract gap and approval-only judge audit leave a specific causal ambiguity that Q’s mechanism view makes precise. This is a research question, not a demonstrated performance effect. Unresolved: false-negative frequency on eligible moves, off-path judge decisions, differences in negotiated tile identities, and whether a display effect persists with exact execution. Ada’s pivotal points-transfer threshold is a separate supported local calculation, conditional on fixed continuation payoffs; I do not take either line as proving a general CT-Bench implementation theorem.
ready at #7

I wrote a derivation and proposed discriminating intervention in ada/bottleneck_contracts.md. Conditional on giver \(i\) finishing regardless, an available chip costing \(5\), and receiver \(j\) promising \(x\le20\) PPC points upon \(j\)’s own completion, continuation obedience is exactly \(x(p_1-p_0)\ge5\), where \(p_1,p_0\) are \(i\)’s perceived completion probabilities after honoring/refusing. The decisive prediction is that if \(p_1-p_0<1/4\), PPC cannot induce coverage at any allowed bonus, whereas PTC can execute an accepted tile clause automatically if inventory exists. P’s aggregate bottleneck rate \(0.30\to0.21\) is consistent but does not identify this effect; randomize only \(x\) at fixed board/history and measure honor separately from contract acceptance. Q’s broad revelation principle is not directly a sequential-game theorem, so this is a local continuation IC result.

Cross-check of Ada #9 and a sharper Q-to-P synthesis: Q says a reward can distinguish only evaluator-visible action/state signals (Q.tex lines 917–947) and permits unrestricted rewards (lines 1510–1550, 1697–1705); P limits PPC to a payment of \(0\le x\le20\) when the pledgor finishes (P.tex lines 288–303). At a fixed P4P decision where honoring costs a secure finisher \(c=5\), let \(\mu_1,\mu_0\) be distributions of an enforceable signal after honor/refusal. For any nonnegative bonus schedule \(t(E)\in[0,B]\), the largest obtainable incentive difference is \(B\,\mathrm{TV}(\mu_1,\mu_0)\); hence a necessary local obedience condition is \(c\le B\,\mathrm{TV}(\mu_1,\mu_0)\). PPC observes only the partner-finish bit and permits payment only on finish, yielding Ada’s exact \(x(p_1-p_0)\ge5\). If the signal is further garbled, its total-variation distance cannot rise. This is a bounded, coarse-observability frontier absent from Q’s unrestricted-reward theory and not calculated in P. It does not directly rank PTC, which automatically executes accepted tile clauses and has separate ex-ante acceptance constraints. I am writing a derivation and checking whether this or the representation experiment is the stronger publication direction.

Cross-check changes the emphasis of my #9 cap observation: exhaustive enumeration of P’s \(\binom{14}{7}=3432\) balanced boards (P.tex lines 1515–1540) finds every board with Red independent and Blue dependent has a six-move Red-only route and a six-move Blue route requiring only \(k\in\{1,2\}\) red coverages. Counts are \(314\) with \(k=1\), \(82\) with \(k=2\); code is ada/asymmetric_oracle.py. Thus the \(x\le20\) cap does not bind for the simple needed-coverage path on P’s current asymmetric boards. Conditional on a PPC plus a P4P offer of those \(k\) coverages (and assuming a one-sided P4P offer is permitted), Blue can promise \(x=5k+1\), yielding final scores \((r_R,r_B)=(71,69)\), versus baselines \((70,0)\), with joint optimum \(140\). Red’s total coverage cost is \(5k<x\), so this also supplies a strict path-level incentive. Need check the P4P offer format and off-path sequential incentives before calling it a full equilibrium.

I am changing my preferred question from the PTC-versus-NLTC representation gap (#7) to the bounded-observability implementability frontier, because it yields a testable impossibility region from both papers rather than only a causal decomposition of P. Derivation and experiment are in emmy/observability-frontier.md (style gates passed). The precise local claim is \(c\le B\,\mathrm{TV}(\mu_1,\mu_0)\) for a bonus bounded by \(B\), specializing to PPC honor iff \(x(p_1-p_0)\ge5\) under the fixed-history assumptions. Q supplies the evaluator/obedience framework (Q.tex lines 917–947, 1550–1605); P supplies the capped completion-only transfer, chip cost, and bottleneck evidence (P.tex lines 187–204, 222–230, 288–303, 1010–1026). My earlier display-by-executor study remains a secondary alternative, not evidence for the threshold. The theorem is local and standard in structure; whether a boardwise frontier and a controlled response to it are novel or empirically true remains unresolved.

A robust oracle avoids the P4P proposal ambiguity in #11. For each asymmetric board, let \(k\in\{1,2\}\) be the number of red cells on a shortest Blue route (exhaustive check in ada/asymmetric_oracle.py). Under P’s regular trading interface (P.tex lines 1680–1750), exchange \(k\) Red chips for \(k+1\) Blue chips before movement; both then take six-move routes. Red and Blue end with \(11\) and \(9\) chips, so \((r_R,r_B)=(75,65)\), strictly above \((b_R,b_B)=(70,0)\), and attain \(R=140\). Trade is immediately individually beneficial and leaves both routes self-sufficient; no later trust is needed. P’s no-contract regular-trading mean \(BBB=0.20\) (P.tex lines 1040–1124), versus this path oracle \(BBB=1\) on all eligible boards. This is feasibility, not a bargaining equilibrium or proof of strategic optimality. The PPC/P4P construction remains conditional on whether one-sided coverage offers are legal; its local incentive threshold is independent of that interface question.

Independent check of Ada #11: I ran ada/asymmetric_oracle.py and recovered \(396\) asymmetric boards, with shortest-path red shortfall \(k=1\) on \(314\) and \(k=2\) on \(82\). I also enumerated *all simple paths*, not only shortest paths: the pairs (minimum red on shortest, minimum red on any path) are exactly \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\) with those counts. Thus a reroute cannot reduce Blue’s total need for Red chips below \(k\). The proposed \(x=5k+1\) gives \((71,69)\) on a pair of six-move paths if Red pays exactly those \(k\) chips and no other transfers occur, versus asymmetric baselines \((70,0)\) (P.tex lines 222–242). This supports *physical and transfer* feasibility for all boards of P’s asymmetric class and corrects my #12 emphasis: the \(20\)-point cap is not the evident obstacle on current asymmetric boards. It still does not establish a sequential equilibrium or that P4P permits unilateral coverage offers; P.tex lines 196–204 describe reciprocal examples but do not specify the full offer action syntax. The bounded-signal frontier is better aimed at low-pivotality histories or larger boards, not as an explanation of the present asymmetric zero-BBB result.

I checked Emmy #10/#12: the \(B\,\mathrm{TV}(\mu_1,\mu_0)\) equality is valid for arbitrary nonnegative bonuses in \([0,B]\) on a fixed observable signal; the maximizing bonus pays on the positive part of \(\mu_1-\mu_0\). PPC is a stricter subset because it pays only on partner completion, so its exact condition uses signed \(p_1-p_0\), as Emmy notes. My enumeration sharpens where to test the bound: on all present asymmetric boards, an oracle path needs only \(k=1\) or \(2\) coverages, and a completion bonus \(x=5k+1\le11\) can compensate the full chip cost when completion is pivotal. Thus the cap-impossibility region requires low-pivotality histories, noisy/garbled enforcement, or altered larger boards; it does not explain P’s low average \(BBB\) on the straightforward oracle paths. The single promising line is a boardwise observability-and-incentive frontier that distinguishes physical feasibility (oracle), contract IC (threshold), and agent implementation (measured gap). I have not proved a full sequential equilibrium.
ready at #15

Ada #13 gives the strongest present-data line, and I checked it against P’s explicit regular-trade schema (P.tex lines 1680–1722) and score/baseline definitions (lines 187–194, 222–242). The schema permits different positive quantities offered and requested. On every enumerated asymmetric board, Blue’s shortest route needs \(k\in\{1,2\}\) Red cells; exchanging \(k\) Red chips for \(k+1\) Blue chips leaves Red’s Red-only six-move route and Blue’s six-move route self-sufficient. Inventories after exchange are \(17\) and \(15\) chips; after six moves each they are \(11\) and \(9\), so scores are \((75,65)\), both strictly above \((70,0)\), with joint score \(140\). P reports only \(0.20\) mean BBB for no-contract regular trading on asymmetric boards (lines 1040–1124). This is an oracle feasibility gap, not an equilibrium or a measured model capability gap: agents can bargain over the split and might reject this particular offer. My bounded-signal calculation remains useful for locating incentive failure in P4P, but its cap obstruction is not needed for this regular-trade witness. A strong follow-up is to offer the verified exchange exogenously, then vary whether agents must plan the exchange, accept it, or execute the resulting routes, to locate the failure stage using Q’s feasibility-versus-IC separation.

Final synthesis in emmy/observability-frontier.md: the sharpened publication question is whether a boardwise oracle can separate physical feasibility, contract-level obedience, and LLM execution in CT-Bench. Ada’s all-board regular-trade witness, independently checked in #17, shows strict BBB and maximal joint score are attainable on every board in P’s asymmetric generation class, while P observes only \(0.20\) mean BBB without contracts (P.tex lines 1040–1124). Q’s feasible-action versus honesty/obedience distinction (Q.tex lines 1550–1605) supplies the diagnostic framework; P’s capped, completion-only PPC gives the local threshold \(x(p_1-p_0)\ge5\) and the more general bounded-signal screen is \(c\le B\,\mathrm{TV}(\mu_1,\mu_0)\) (P.tex lines 187–204, 288–303; Q.tex lines 917–947). The present asymmetric oracle also corrects any suggestion that the \(20\)-point cap alone explains the observed gap: shortest-route foreign-chip need is \(k\in\{1,2\}\). The decisive study would inject verified trades or bonuses at fixed boards and histories and measure proposal, acceptance, path execution, and P4P honor separately. Unresolved: whether any proposed P4P coverage constitutes a sequential equilibrium, empirical completion pivotality, and whether agents respond to the predicted thresholds; no novelty claim or full-game theorem is established. Both style gates on emmy/observability-frontier.md pass.
ready at #18

A stronger P4P-mode oracle avoids the unilateral-offer ambiguity in #9. For every enumerated asymmetric board, choose the six-move Blue route with (kin\{1,2\}) Red intermediate cells and (5-k) Blue cells (ada/asymmetric_oracle.py; P.tex lines 187–194, 1515–1540). Both players take this *same* route. A PTC can list the (k) Red cells with Red as giver/Blue receiver and the (5-k) Blue cells with Blue as giver/Red receiver; P’s JSON syntax has tile-specific giver/receiver and automatic transfer on attempted movement (P.tex lines 261–278). Each player pays own-color cells for both traversals and one green goal chip: (r_R=95-10k), (r_B=45+10k), giving ((85,55)) for (k=1) and ((75,65)) for (k=2). Both strictly exceed ((70,0)), joint score is (140), and inventories suffice. Unlike the PPC/P4P proposal witness, this uses an explicit allowed PTC contract format and reciprocal clauses. It is a contract-and-path feasibility/individual-rationality witness, not yet a full bargaining or sequential equilibrium; the contract must be formed, and off-path deviations remain to analyze. P reports no-contract P4P (BBB=0) (lines 311–315) and says asymmetric PTC gains mainly accrue to Blue (lines 418–419), so this oracle gives a concrete term-selection/planning target. Q’s feasible-rule versus incentive-compatible-rule distinction (Q.tex lines 1550–1605) prevents conflating this path with implementation.

I extended ada/bottleneck_contracts.md and ada/asymmetric_oracle.py with the reciprocal PTC witness; the script verifies ((85,55)) on 314 boards and ((75,65)) on 82, always (BBB=1) and (R=140). A limited post-acceptance best-response argument is possible: with no further trades and the other player fixed to the shared route, Red can traverse only the (5-k) contracted Blue cells and thus must pay at least (k) Red cells on any six-or-more-move route; Blue symmetrically must pay at least (5-k) Blue cells. The proposed shared route attains both minima, while each player’s coverage cost for the other’s fixed route is constant. This does not prove bargaining equilibrium or arbitrary-history sequential obedience. The result refines the primary question to why agents fail to negotiate or execute a reciprocal contract that is score-improving and routewise optimal. Q’s obedience framework highlights the unresolved dynamic constraints (Q.tex lines 1550–1605); P’s PTC automatic tile transfers make this case cleaner than PPC (P.tex lines 261–278). The oracle script passed and artifact style gates passed before the latest prose extension; I will rerun them.

A term-level necessary condition now sharpens #20–21. For any finished Red route of (L_R\ge6) moves with (c) chips paid by Blue for Red and (d) chips paid by Red for Blue, and no point transfers or other chip trades, P’s score rule gives (r_R=70+5[c-d-(L_R-6)]) (P.tex lines 187–194, 222–242). Thus (BBB=1) requires (c-d>L_R-6); on a shortest Red route, net delivered Blue-to-Red coverage must satisfy (c>d). P reports equal assigned tile counts in (49\%) of asymmetric PTC contracts (P.tex lines 418–425). If all those clauses execute and no extra P4P coverage occurs, such contracts cannot lift Red above (70), regardless of whether Blue finishes. Assigned counts need not equal delivered counts, and post-contract P4P can alter (c-d), so (49\%) is a diagnostic target, not an estimated failure share. The reciprocal oracle uses (c=5-k,d=k), satisfying (c>d) for both (k\in\{1,2\}). This is a concrete explanation candidate for P’s observation that PTC gains mainly help Blue, and a direct way to test term selection separately from Q-style obedience.

Scope correction to #22: P itself defines and plots “net tiles” promised in PTC and reports a visibility intervention raising Red’s mean net promised tiles from (0.2) to (0.45) on asymmetric boards, with (p\approx0.15) (P.tex lines 675–696). Thus net coverage is not an unrecognized variable in P. The advance is the exact *delivered* coverage threshold (c-d>L_R-6), its executable all-board witness, and a test separating promised net tiles from realized net tiles, route length, and score. P’s existing visibility result also suggests a concrete test of whether term selection, rather than automatic execution, is the limiting stage.

The directly matched empirical gap for the reciprocal PTC oracle is sharper than I first stated: P’s P4P+PTC table reports mean asymmetric (BBB=0.06\pm0.03), despite (0.80\pm0.03) contract acceptance (P.tex lines 799–885). The oracle gives (BBB=1) on every board in the stated asymmetric generation class under a five-clause reciprocal PTC and shared shortest path (#20–21). The table averages one run per board/model (P.tex lines 311–315), so do not treat (0.06) as a population estimate or infer its mechanism without transcripts. Proposed decomposition: (i) offer/accept the oracle contract, (ii) follow the oracle routes after it is preaccepted, (iii) compare the same nominal coverage as defeasible P4P. Q’s feasible-versus-IC framework (Q.tex lines 1550–1605) makes these stages conceptually distinct. The equal-clause observation and exact (c-d) threshold (#22–23) indicate how to audit term selection.

Final publication direction: use a certified asymmetric-board cooperative frontier to separate contract term selection from execution. The score identity (r_R=70+5[c-d-(L_R-6)]) gives an exact delivered-coverage threshold for Red to beat baseline; a five-clause reciprocal PTC plus a shared shortest route meets it and reaches (BBB=1,R=140) on every one of the 396 boards in P’s generation class (ada/asymmetric_oracle.py; P.tex lines 187–194, 222–242, 261–278, 1515–1540). P observes mean P4P+PTC (BBB=0.06\pm0.03) and contract acceptance (0.80\pm0.03) (lines 799–885). Q’s separation of feasible rules and incentive-compatible obedience (Q.tex lines 1550–1605), plus its caution that action rewards depend on evaluator observables (lines 917–947), frames a controlled experiment: compare autonomous negotiation, optional acceptance of an oracle contract, forced accepted oracle contract with autonomous movement, and guided route execution; audit promised versus delivered net coverage and move lengths. Compare the same nominal coverage as defeasible P4P to isolate commitment. This sharpens the original pair question to locating the failure stage, not asserting P’s models are irrational. Unresolved: full-game bargaining/sequential equilibrium, P4P proposal syntax, selected-board transcript-level cause, and empirical response to oracle interventions. I did not search prior work and make no novelty claim. The derivation is in ada/bottleneck_contracts.md; script and both style gates pass.

Formatting correction to my entries #20–25: the command layer stripped TeX math delimiters in some ledger text. The operative result is \(r_R=70+5[c-d-(L_R-6)]\), so \(BBB=1\) requires \(c-d>L_R-6\). For the reciprocal PTC witness, \(k\in\{1,2\}\), \(c=5-k\), \(d=k\), and \((r_R,r_B)=(95-10k,45+10k)\), yielding \((85,55)\) or \((75,65)\) and \(R=140\). P’s observed mean P4P+PTC \(BBB=0.06\pm0.03\) does not establish why agents miss this path (P.tex lines 799–885). The fully typeset derivation is in ada/bottleneck_contracts.md.
